utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday, the 6th of March, 2008. Good afternoon to the Prosecution, to Mr. Seselj, and to everyone assisting us in this case. Today we'll proceed with the cross-examination of the witness. I believe that Mr. Seselj has one hour and three minutes left. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Seselj, and of course I'd like to greet the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kulic, today we'll go through your statement which you made to The Hague investigators on the 14th of November, 2007. Why did you say that General Dusan Pekic in 1991 was the Minister of the Interior and commanded the police forces in Federal Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was the information I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it was common knowledge in the then-Yugoslavia that the federal minister for the police was General Petar Gracanin at that time. Dusan Pekic retired much earlier as a general and national hero, and he was a high-ranking official of the veterans association. From whom did you get this erroneous information?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I received this information from people who went to Belgrade, had contacts, quoted authorities most probably regarding information from the association of Serbs in Belgrade. But I can't be sure what the names are of the persons who misinformed me in this way. But it was certainly someone who was linked to the events in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were misled in this respect. Were you also misled when you were given the information that Ilija Sasic was, as you say, a significant figure and as such participated in negotiations with Franjo Tudjman concerning the release of some men who were arrested, that is, Zeljko Rozantovic, Arkan, and another one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you misled there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't Ilija Sacic but Ilija Sasic. And when it comes to him it's well known that at the time he was the president of the regional organisation of the SDS, at least that's what his colleagues from the SDS told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And why did you link Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Razantovic at the time when they were not arrested at the same place at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the media at the time in Croatia I had occasion both to see and to hear subsequently that Mr. Sasic participated in the search for a solution as to the release of those men because they had been arrested by the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ilijas Sasic only negotiated about the release of Goran Hadzicic. He had nothing to do with the arrest of Zeljko Rozantovic, Arkan, nor did Arkan have anything to do with Western Slavonia. You never saw one of Arkan's men in Western Slavonia. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Seselj is right when he says this, but as regards the arrests and negotiations I had information for which I could not verify the source, but they came from the media concerning the arrest of both men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how can you now comment on my assertion that not in a single medium was it ever broadcast or published that Sasic had anything to do with negotiations concerning Arkan's release?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow that Mr. Seselj may be right. I assume he's more familiar with the facts of this case than I am. But I simply gave the information I gleaned from the media. I didn't have any sources I can document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned Jovan Kulic during your examination-in-chief. Are you related to Jovan Kulic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not related to Jovan Kulic, and the first time I saw him was in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And whose volunteer was he in?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to the best of my knowledge he was a volunteer who came from the Republic of Serbia, somewhere around Novi Sad. And whose volunteer he was. I'm not certain, but I thought he belonged to the same group of volunteers who had arrived just before Kulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you link him to the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed he belonged to it, but he didn't necessarily have to belong to it. I did not obtain information concerning his political affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this was just an assumption on your part, right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke of the volunteers as a single group and I felt that they were consistent and unified group, and I still think that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please give the witness document number 1 and put it on the ELMO. I hope that the members of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor have got this document. It's document number 1 and it consists of two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, would you be so kind as to read this document. It's a new statement by Colonel Jovan Trbojevic. I received it today. Please be kind enough, just without the preamble, just "I state the following ..." If you can.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I state the following: From 1986 onwards I served in Novi Sad as an officer, a colonel of the JNA, commander of the Territorial Defence Staff of the town of Novi Sad. On the 1st of November, 1991, I was summoned to the General Staff of the JNA in Belgrade where I was told that I had been transferred from Novi Sad to the garrison in Pakrac in Western Slavonia. I assumed my new duty on the 5th of November, 1991. As the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff of Novi Sad, Jovan Kulic approached me, asking me to help him finance per diem payments for his fighters. He introduced himself to me as a captain and the commander of a group of fighters from Novi Sad. He told me he had a unit of 40 men. I remember this was in early September 1991. As of the 5th of November, 1991, I lost contact with Jovan Kulic. After the liberation of Vukovar, Jovan Kulic arrived in Novi Sad and went to the regional staff of the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina and approached Colonel Milutin Lazetic who was an operative of the regional staff of the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina, asking him to get him a pass so that he could go to Western Slavonia via Banja Luka and Okucani with his volunteers on the territory where I was the commander. If I remember correctly Jovan Kulic and his unit arrived in Western Slavonia on the 25 of November, 1991. I deployed him in the village of Mijokovicevo. This is a village and a mountain pass on the Daruvar-Vidovica road. I disbanded the Territorial Defence in Western Slavonia on the 24th of December, 1991, and went to Banja Luka. Lower ranking units were transferred into JNA units so that the staffs and units of the Territorial Defence were dissolved. I know for certain that Jovan Kulic and his unit remained in that area for several months, but what he was doing there and under whose orders I do not know. To clarify, Jovan Kulic left Mijokovicevo on my orders on the 12th of December, 1991, and went with his unit to the village of Kusonje near Pakrac. When leaving the village of Mijokovicevo, Jovan Kulic was wounded in the shoulder. I wish to mention that Jovan Kulic and his unit was sent to area of Western Slavonia by the regional staff of the Territorial Defence Vojvodina. After the wartime events Jovan Kulic applied to me asking me to give him a certificate stating that he had been a fighter in Western Slavonia and to issue a certificate of wounding so that he could claim his entitlements. Jovan Kulic now lives in the village of Ratkovo in the municipality of Odzaci. Previously he lived in Novi Sad and he was a house painter. I know that he was born in Ruma and he comes from Lika originally. I'm giving this statement of my own free will. I assert under full liability that everything I have stated is correct and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I cannot finish reading because it's too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you see that this is certified by the court in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt this statement by Colonel Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't doubt it for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So now you're convinced that this is a true statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that Jovan Kulic had nothing to do with volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party but that rather he arrived as a volunteer of the Territorial Defence of Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've just realised what Jovan Kulic's role really was in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honours, that you will find this information useful concerning the group in Novi Sad mentioned by Witness Teunens which was tried before the court in Banja Luka, so please bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You stated to The Hague investigators that the paramilitary formations were financed from three sources: enterprises or companies, political parties, and the church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember everything I said in my statement, but I assume that's what I said because I still believe this, Your Honours. This is the information that reached me from the people I was in contact with in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You stated that Seselj's Radical Party, the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Renewal Movement received donations from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I don't see the statement in front of me so I can't confirm I said that. But this is right, it's correct. I had this information and it's still the information I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have any information that the Serbian Radical Party in 1991, which was when it was established and registered, or in 1992 or 1993 received a single donation of any kind from abroad? Do you have any data on this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I can't support this with data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you said that off the top of your head. Well, where did you get the information that the church financed paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Financing of the formations participating in the war at the time is something I learned about only in the staff of Western Slavonia. There were people there who went to Banja Luka or to Belgrade. So it's second-hand information. I don't have any specific information to show this; otherwise, I would have adduced it with my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how can you accuse the church without any specific information? The church sent humanitarian aid to people who needed it and to people who were wounded, and this was food, clothes, and so on. Never did the church give a single dinar to buy weapons or to finance the military, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I believe Mr. Seselj, but my experience in the area where I was and relations with the church authorities was somewhat different. I wish to distance myself from that part of the statement where Mr. Seselj's party's mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm surprised by one thing. In the statement from 2002 you said, "I'm not sure whether Vuk Draskovic was the leader of the White Eagles." That's on page 11. "I think the White Eagles belonged to Seselj. In fact, my wife, who at that time was employed in the Vocin medical centre, told me that the volunteers belonged to the paramilitary formation called White Eagles." And then in your statement of 2007 you leave this out. "I think the White Eagles belong to Seselj." So what is left is - and that's paragraph 41 - "I'm not sure whether Vuk Draskovic was the leader of the Beli Orlovi, or the White Eagles. It is in fact my wife who worked at the medical centre in Vocin at the time who told me that the volunteers belong to Beli Orlovi paramilitary organisation. So how did it come about that in 2002 you say that you think the volunteers, the White Eagles, belonged to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have to slow down. The interpreters can't follow you, and so we get nothing out of your questions, and less even out of the answers from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How is it possible, then, that in 2002 you ascribe the White Eagles to me and in the statement from 2007 you leave this out and you no longer ascribe the White Eagles to me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the concept of White Eagles really existed, but it belonged to a certain group of volunteers. And I didn't have any special formal contacts in my work with them, but names of political leaders were bandied about who were behind this recruitment of volunteer units. I cannot assert decidedly that they belonged to anyone because I don't have any first-hand evidence, but it's evident that they were there in the Vocin area. And any unintentional statement concerning anyone, including Mr. Seselj, well, I apologise, I really didn't intend because I wasn't sure. So I left your name out because I wasn't absolutely certain who was the person who might be said to have participated in recruiting these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that the killing of the Croatian civilians in Vocin, that in that killing a man called Simic from Vocin took part, but before that you said that in addition to Simic there was a man called Ivanovic from Popovci. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, why did you mention these Ivanovici people from Popovci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention a single name yesterday, Your Honour, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about your testimony in the Milosevic trial? You mentioned Simic and you mentioned the Jovanovics.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then why have you forgotten them now, if you speak about the Simics, Vocin, and the Jovanovics from Popovaci as participating in the killing of Croatian civilians in Vocin, why have you left them out now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me explain this. Of the two young men in the group who had contacts with the villagers that recognised them, they mentioned a young boy from Simici - and I'll quote -- try and quote what the people said - and a small -- and a small boy from Ivanovici. Now, when they tried to establish this it turned out that one of the brothers, or they were the children of a family named Simic, and another son from the other Ivanovici family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You spoke about Rajko Bojicic yesterday and accused him of killing one of the four young Croats. Rajko Bojicic contacted me and - might be witness Mr. Kulic be provided with document number 2 - he contacted me and I received a statement that was certified at the fourth municipal court in Belgrade. It is from Rajko Bojicic. Now, would you read that statement out, please. Out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Last night I looked at the footing from the legal proceedings against Dr. Seselj in The Hague, and provoked by the lies told by Mladen Kulic I was prompted to tell you the truth about the events that were discussed. At the time I was the assistant commander for operations and training in the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Podravska Slatina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down, to read more slowly. It is impossible to follow at this rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, again you're reading out too quickly and the result is that the interpretation is impossible. So I would kindly ask you to read it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. "Last night I looked at the footage from the trial of Dr. Vojislav Seselj at the Hague Tribunal, and provoked by the lies that witness Mladen Kulic told, I wish to tell the truth about the events that were discussed. At that time I was an assistant to the commander for operative and training affairs in the staff of the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina municipality. I state with full responsibility that Mladen Kulic, when he arrived in the territory of the Territorial Defence staff of Podravska Slatina, performed organisational and mobilisational work. He took in and deployed the first volunteers that arrived and sent them to units and formations of the Territorial Defence. After that, in the aim of ensuring combat operations, he conducted reconnaissance work, reconnoitring, communications with the village of Ceralije, village of Lipovac, village of Ivanbreg, and the roads to Podravska Slatina and Ceralije village and Podravska Slatina and Ivanbreg village. On the basis of that reconnaissance work pursuant to his orders an ambush was organised along the Slatina-Ivanbreg road, and in this combat operation Zvonimir Cubelic was killed, while Branko Sikic was wounded. Witness Mladen Kulic after that boasted and said how capable he was and tried to raise the respect he never had, because everybody knew that he was -- there was a criminal report against him, (redacted) (redacted), and that he was very aggressive and prone to various incidents, which is why he was not appointed to a post that would otherwise correspond to his rank." Your Honours, I cannot accept reading this pamphlet anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll redact this part of the transcript. (redacted), but please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I asked the witness to read out the whole of the statement. He refused to read it out. So I have to read it out, Judge, if you agree, or we're going to force the witness to do so. I would prefer it if you would force the witness to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He does not want to so we're not going to force him to read it out. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: A short remark. In the transcript Mr. Seselj said: "You spoke about Rajko Bojicic yesterday and accused him of killing one of the four young Croats." As far as I remember, and I checked the transcript, the witness never said that Rajko Bojicic was involved in the killing; he only said that he would take him responsible if the fate of these young Croats would not be found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, let's try not to waste any time. You have got the statement in your own language, this statement given by Rajko Bojicic, and you can put questions to the witness on the basis of this statement, saying, for example, He said this and this in the statement and what do you have to say. Because if we read the entire statement, it's going to take a lot of time, whereas you only want to point out two or three items in this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I said that this witness accused Rajko Bojicic of being responsible for the death of the four Croatian young men. Now, what it says in the transcript, I don't know. What the interpreter said, I don't know. You have my recording in Serbian and you can check that out, but that's what I said. Secondly, earlier on in some situations I highlighted certain portions of the statement, but this particular statement is very important because there was a lot of talk about Rajko Bojicic here and his role, so I'd like to read the statement in its entirety. It's just a page and a half so it will last four minutes, 23 seconds. "While I was watching the broadcast of the trial last night, it was interesting for me to note that Mladen Kulic, according to his own words, was in all the places where some crimes happened to have been committed, or as he says he heard about them, which logically leads us to conclude that he must have participated in that. Specifically, when he spoke about the house of the Matanci house which was attacked and torched as soon as night fell, he confirmed that he was present because otherwise those three young men who committed that act would not have been able to set aside that house as the object of their attack because they don't know the area. They could especially not know which house belonged to a Serb family and which to a Croatian unless Mladen Kulic pointed that out to them. Otherwise at that time everybody talk about the fact that Mladen Kulic was present during the event as the initiator of the torching of the Matanci house. Furthermore, when he spoke about the four young men who were killed, he did not say that they were members of the Territorial Defence and that they were performing duties to secure the rear, or rather that we did not send them up to the front line precisely to avoid somebody killing them because they were Croats. Otherwise, in the Territorial Defence you did not have exclusively Serbs. In the command part there were Croats, too. For example, Lieutenant Darbos, there were some Muslims too. An example is Captain Fadil. I cannot remember his surname. He was their chief. "Mladen Kulic also said that he, when this killing took place, was on leave because he was visiting his family in Belgrade. It is true that he left the area of the Territorial Defence staff of Podravska Slatina, but it seems amazing when we heard his explanation that from Banja Luka he returned to Vocin allegedly to link up some things for the children of his friends. And how come when he returned he happened to come across mothers who were crying in front of a clinic? It is logical that somebody must have pointed those young men out to him. And through yesterday's testimony Mladen Kulic confirmed the suspicions of the time, which are that he took part in the organisation of all those and other crimes, and he didn't -- his conduct did not follow the instructions of the security organs because as a security officer he must have interrupted his visit and taken part in the investigations and establishing the circumstances and the facts under which these killings took place, because it was the area -- his area of responsibility, whereas immediately after that he returned probably to Banja Luka or Belgrade straight away. "As the commander I took all the necessary measures and sent a security officer and an intelligence organ, an assistant commander for morale and political guidance, to establish" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to remind that cross-examination, the purpose of cross-examination is putting questions and not reading out long submissions. I think we should stop this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mussemeyer, Mr. Seselj needs to put a question. But if you put a question, you need to get some understanding of the document which is unfortunately in Serbian and it has not been translated. So somebody has to read it. You could have read it, the witness could have read it, but the witness does not wish to. I could have read it but I don't speak the language. So the only person who can read it is the accused, so that's what he's doing. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I have to present this document and then ask my questions. The document arrived today. You can see from the fax number at the top of the page, when the document arrived. "A unit was sent from the police station in Vocin with their commander so that they could help in the investigation of the act mentioned and that they should urgently inform what the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina -- they should report urgently on what they were doing. It is not true that the command of the staff of Western Slavonia was not informed, the Banja Luka Corps and the relevant authorities in the government of the Republic of Serbia. "On the 3rd of December I went in Podravska Slatina to Belgrade and personally informed them there about the event. This terrible act had a shocking affect on the fighters and their morale and introduced fear and uncertainty amongst all the members of the Territorial Defence, because it was obvious to them that nobody was protected. "By his testimony last night Kulic attempted in actual fact to justify himself, claiming that everything that he spoke about was something that he heard from somebody else and on the basis of those stories drew his own conclusions, whereas the essence of the matter is that he participated in all those events, which was common knowledge in this territory and which he himself confirmed, just as he confirmed his status in Croatia in which he lives quite normally and where he was not held responsible for a single act as opposed to others who were and who were tried even in absentia for the mere fact that they had taken part in an armed support against paramilitary forces of Croatia. "I personally met Radovan Novacic and a group of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who were in the village of Lager Sekulinci where they joined up the units of the Territorial Defence straight away under the command of the command staff of the TO and the command of the detachment of the TO whose tasks they carried high in disciplined fashion and set an example to all other men. "I give this statement of my own accord and agree that Dr. Vojislav Seselj can use it before the International Tribunal in The Hague, in Belgrade the 6th of March 2008, Rajko Bojicic. Mr. Kulic, is this assertion made Rajko Bojicic true and correct, that in the Territorial Defence, in addition to Serbs there were also Croats and even Muslims? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, Your Honour, in the part in which it says that Mr. Fadil was in the command. Now, as to the other members it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of a Lieutenant Darbos, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Darbos was not a Croat but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what is he ethnically speaking?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Darbos was from a mixed family and he joined the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember these four young men who were killed, they were from mixed marriages too, at least some of them. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that is true. I don't think that holds true for any of those young men. And apropos of that the statement that was read out a moment ago by Dr. Seselj, he is mixing up some dates in flagrant fashion. The 3rd of December was five days before the two young men disappeared, for your information. So it is quite obvious that there's something wrong with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, when did those men young men disappear?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Exactly the day when you fled from Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not flee from Western Slavonia and I reject that insinuation with indignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did you go to Belgrade with on the 8th of December, Mr. Kulic, then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on my own, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In one car?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who was in the other car that was with you? Who was in that second car?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, among others, Your Honours, that day there was Mr. Rajko Bojicic with his driver and we met up in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Savo Radosevic go with his wife Jelena in this second car?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went on that day, too, that's the truth, but they didn't go with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You moved in a column.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber's legal officer has just told me that there are people in the public gallery so the damage might have been done already. Let's please move into private session for this part of the testimony, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say at that my intention here is to catch the witness lying as often as I can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my defence case and I have proof. You can get rid of all the evidence afterwards, but I'm going to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, do you know who Pajo Baljak is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I knew who Pajo Baljak was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean you knew? You don't know now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the lapse of time, I don't know if I could even recognise him. I haven't seen him since 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind as to give the witness document number 3, it's a very short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You probably won't have problems reading this because Pajo Baljak speaks highly of you in this statement which was certified in the municipal court in Ruma this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before addressing this statement, I don't know what it contains. I would like to get back to the murder of the four boys in Vocin. According to the written testimony which the Prosecution received from Mr. Vasic this morning, it seems that according to this statement you took part in this murder because you were present. Do you dispute this? Do you accept this? What is your position? We have not your reaction on this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll repeat that part of my statement. On the 8th of December, when preparing to travel to visit my family, quite by chance I ran into a group of women who were crying, who were weeping. I asked them why they were crying. They said that their children were missing. I did not know there was a group that was working. But to help those women get information I took them to the staff and I asked the man who wrote this statement, if he wrote it, Rajko Bojicic, because he was the staff commander, I asked him to explain to these women where their children were, to tell them where they were. In this statement Mr. Bojicic mentions some flagrantly inaccurate pieces of information, but he says that he was responsible at the time and that he did take some action. I don't know whether he did or not, but I know that he left Vocin on the 8th of December and never came back again. He was not present at the exodus. That's for Mr. Seselj's information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, like everyone else, I listened to the statement. There's a point of detail which he mentioned. He said that you were a security officer at the time and as such you should have begun an investigation and that was part of your responsibility. That's what he said. And as far as he is concerned he said he forwarded the information to Banja Luka. Was this true, that you were in charge of security matters at the time and you had the power or the authority to conduct an investigation? If that was the case, why didn't you do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was never the security organ, either of that Territorial Defence staff or of lower units. It's -- lower level units. It's partly true that I worked on organisation because I had to receive new people and find them accommodation, so that's partly true. But that I was in charge of reconnaissance and security affairs, that is not correct. There were other people in charge of that. And let me tell you in passing I would ask Your Honours to obtain the indictment in Croatia concerning Mr. Bojicic's activities, where regardless of Mr. Seselj's insinuation, I never participated, nor will I ever participate, not just in the case of Mr. Bojicic but in case of anyone of those members, but I will always speak the truth as I experienced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We don't know Mr. Bojicic. We just heard about him right now. Has there been an indictment issued against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was he charged with, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was accused of command responsibility and some individual crimes, but as a commander he is responsible for events -- well, the events we have spoken about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened in the end? Was he convicted? Was he acquitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the proceedings of the district court I'm not familiar with them. But it's now available to the public, both in Serbia and in Croatia, to see who has been indicted in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you be so kind, Mr. Kulic, as to read Tomo Baljak's statement. You can start from the second paragraph because the first one contains his personal details.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "After the beginning of the war clashes in Croatia in 1991, I was in the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When the war broke out in Croatia in 1991 I was in the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina. First I was in the village of Sekulinci and then I moved to the village of Ceralije. I am a hunter. I was employed in the forestry service for 23 years so that for more than two months in the course of September and October 1991, as a member of the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina, I carried my hunting rifle which fired shot. I am certain that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in the autumn of 1991, in October or early November, arrived in Sekulinci. Their leader was Radovan Novacic. The SRS volunteers were extremely disciplined. Correct. And they were polite to the local population. They helped the local people in harvesting corn and doing other farm work. Drinking alcohol was strictly prohibited to them. On one occasion I offered the volunteers some brandy as refreshment. Radovan Novacic told me not to do that anymore; otherwise, he would send the men back to Serbia if he learns that the volunteers drank alcohol. I also saw personally the volunteers doing gymnastics in the morning, according to all the rules of soldiering. I assert with full liability that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party did not participate in the commission of any crimes but exclusively in combat activities as ordered by the competent command of the JNA. I know Mladen Kulic personally from the time when we lived in Podravska Slatina. I know that before the war he was the director of the Univerzal company. After the persecution of the Serbs in Croatia began, Kulic came from Podravska Slatina to Vocin where he was accommodated in the home of Nikola Radosevic, the brother of Savo Radosevic. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall redact this. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to make an observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pajo Baljak only signed this statement. Unlike Dr. Seselj I know Pajo Baljak. His vocabulary and his linguistic skills would not permit him to write in this way. This was produced in the offices of the Serbian Radical Party to help this man. That's what I think, Dr. Seselj, and if I may address him directly, Your Honours. But I assume this also is part of the rights of the accused, to mistreat like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will draw its conclusions, but you are saying that her intellect was such that she could not express herself so well. I think we've understood this. So please finish the reading of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't agree with this. I don't think we should continue reading this statement because there are constant personal references made and we are not in private session. So I disagree here. I would also like to mention that these people -- well, Mr. Seselj can call these people to come and testify, because if they testify, their testimony will undoubtedly be relevant and important for the Bench. But as far as I'm concerned these statements have no probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what do you have to respond, what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am presenting these statements as documents in my cross-examination so that I can base questions to the witness on them and so that the witness can give his opinion on the facts mentioned in the statements. They do not have any probative value in themselves, and neither do the 92 ter statements that will be presented to you. It's all one and the same thing. This statement may have been drawn up by my legal advisors based on their conversation with Pajo Baljak, just as the OTP does in the case of their witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I'm interrupting you but I am very careful -- listening very carefully to what you say, every word, every comma. But you have just mentioned false witnesses. There are no false witnesses. What you can say is Prosecution witnesses who don't seem to be true witnesses. But when you talk about false witnesses you seem to be indicating that the Trial Chamber accepts the testimony of false witnesses, which is something I am dead against. I think it's important to mention this. Just say that the Prosecution is calling witnesses, who according to you are false witnesses, but you cannot say that false witnesses come and testify before this Bench. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, but I hesitate to get up and deal with a witness my colleague has been dealing with. But really, for the benefit of the record, this practice must, in our respectful submission, stop. There is simply no basis for statements of third witnesses to be read into the record by other witnesses as a basis for cross-examination. Certainly if the Prosecution asked Witness A to read the statements of Witness B into the record, that would not be tolerated. There are ways of using these statements to cross-examine this witness but that does not necessarily entail asking the witness to read someone else's statement into the record. What's happening here, in effect, is a process by which Dr. Seselj is attempting to get the statements or testimony of other witnesses before the Trial Chamber without allowing the Prosecution the benefit of cross-examine these witnesses, without allowing the Trial Chamber to determine whether these witnesses gave these statements freely, voluntarily. These are simply documents that purport to be the truth which he's then asking this witness to read into the record with no indication at all for the purpose to which this information is being used. Simply a statement that it goes to the cross-examination. Well, he can -- Dr. Seselj, with all due respect, can take anything contained in that statement and put it to this witness in the form of a simple question. He doesn't need to have the witness read into the record a lengthy statement that may or may not be written by the purported author and for which we can't cross-examine, the Chamber can't question the purported author of the document. We have no idea where this information is coming from. And with all due respect, the Prosecution asserts that this process, this procedure, must stop and it must stop right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things, Mr. Mundis. We do not know whether this statement comes from the purported witness. That's what you say. But there is a signature on this statement, there is a stamp, and the statement has been authenticated according to the relevant procedure by the relevant administrative authority. You have a stamp, you have a signature on this statement. We, therefore, can presume or assume that there are indicia of reliability here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting. I might be mistaken, but I'd like to give my opinion on this point. What is certified here is only the signature of the witness, not the statement as such. We only know that this is the certified signature of the person who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Everybody agrees on that. That's what I talked about, indicia of reliability. Now, as far as the substance of the statement is concerned, we have no idea whether the witness is telling the truth or not. However, Mr. Mundis is absolutely right on the second point. Mr. Seselj needs to ask his questions in the following manner: I am putting to you a document drafted by Mr. X on such and such dates. This is a certified document. In this document in the Serbian language the following is stated at paragraph 2. And then, Mr. Seselj, you ask your question. You could have asked, for example, the following: In this document, Mr. X states that you were the one who organised the offensive that led to the death of these four young men. Do you agree or not? And then the witness would have said, No, I do not agree. Mr. Seselj, that's the way you should proceed. You submit the document for everybody to see it and then you say, Such and such a thing is being said in this paragraph of the document. You summarize what is being said - we don't want to spend hours reading other documents - you ask the question and the witness can tell you whether he agrees or not. Please proceed and then the registrar will tell me how much time you have got left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it has been the practice of this Court thus far to proceed in the way I did, that is to say, that in the cross-examination the document is presented to the witness, that they're asked to read out the document and then to answer questions. And I have my own personal experience. That is what Geoffrey Nice did to me in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, the Prosecutor. He put documents before me, documents I had never seen before. He asked me to read them out, and then he asked questions about that. Now if you're changing case law and court practice, then that's another thing. You're the power here. I am just an unprotected accused so I have to follow what you say, and I'm here between the "scylla" and "charybdis."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. You're neither a victim nor anything else and the Tribunal is not the power you're describing. But there's a point where you're right. I've had the opportunity to check this. When you testified in the Milosevic case, Mr. Nice asked you to read out portions of some documents. That's true. Mr. Mundis, what do you have to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Two points, Mr. President. I'm sure I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but Mr. Nice would have shown the accused, Mr. Seselj, documents not signed statements written by other witnesses, number 1. And number 2, if I recall correctly, the Trial Chamber in this case has issued guidelines that cover the cross-examination of witnesses, and paragraph 26 of those guidelines indicates that a party cross-examining a witness may show the witness the information obtained from a previous witness on the condition that the source of the information is not identified. Now, obviously these people, these statements that Dr. Seselj is showing are not previous witnesses, which in and of itself leads to a different problem: The fact that the Prosecution does not have the opportunity to check out this information, to check the validity of this information, to cross-examine these witnesses. We are simply being presented ambush-style with a series of faxed statements coming from Belgrade without the opportunity to review them, to check them, to see if they're accurate. We can't cross-examine them. We can't challenge what the witnesses purport to say in these written statements. It is simply an unfair procedure. And I submit that if the Prosecution were to do the same thing, the Trial Chamber would not allow us to do that. If we were to be putting signed witness statements to Defence witnesses as a means of cross-examining them, I feel relatively confident that this Trial Chamber would not allow us to do that. There are procedures for getting written statements before the Trial Chamber. Those procedures are not followed in this instance where a witness is simply presented with the written statement of someone else and asked to read it into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I would once again like to rely on case law here and practice at this Tribunal. When Slobodan Milosevic called a defence witness - it was a judge from pristine, the investigating judge, Danica Marinkovic, and among others she investigated the Racak affair and many others - she presented a certain number of documents in the courtroom and presented the facts. In the meantime, during the break, over the weekend, Geoffrey Nice found Albanians, individuals of Albanian ethnicity that Danica Mariknovic had mentioned who had given her statements previously and they gave him, Geoffrey Nice, new statements in which they denied what she had said. And he operated with that, Geoffrey Nice, and he operated with, Geoffrey Nice operated with that quite freely in the courtroom. So there's a fact for you. Now, you can change case law here using my case, I don't mind, but it is my aim -- I'm not offering this into evidence. These people are going to come in court to testify and I'm going to have far more defence witnesses, and they'll be testifying 15 minutes, 20 minutes, half an hour with respect to certain facts and circumstances. I'm not going to lose time on negligible issues like the Prosecution is doing. But I would -- in challenging a Prosecution witness, I do have the right to present facts from these statements. Now, when these witnesses come into court then the Prosecution will be able to cross-examine them, because it doesn't matter what it says in the statement here, what is important is what this witness says based on the facts read out from the statement. That's the essence, that's the crux of the matter. And I think I have been able to tackle cross-examination and Anglo-Saxon law very well by now. I'm an amateur. Mr. Mundis should know about that; it's his profession. But I think that I have become quite good at it now. So this is a statement by these witnesses, and when they come into court you'll hear them and hear their testimony. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. The Chamber needs to make a decision on the procedure because my point of view might not be the same as that of my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One remark about what Mr. Seselj said. Please do not quote the case law of the Milosevic trial. It's not part of the case law because the trial was not completed. There was no control afterwards of the transcript. No judgement was rendered by the Judges who would have ruled on the probative value of various documents. Therefore, I would like to ask Mr. Seselj to rely on different case law and not to constantly rely on the case law of the Milosevic case. It's a non-trial, on the non-trial of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Lattanzi, I have to say something before you make a final ruling. I hope I will die innocent like Mr. Milosevic. However, here in this Tribunal we are using documents, transcripts, and other papers that are not complete. At the Slavko Dokmanovic trial, there's a lot of material there, and I've been disclosed a lot of those documents, although a judgement wasn't made in that case either. So these proceedings can't have its own case law independently of other Trial Chambers. And let me take your example to prove my point. You refused to -- you rejected what I said when I said that a witness under 92 ter cannot be partially examined in chief here. Mr. Antonetti said that that was the practice of this Tribunal because that happened in other trials, although you have no grounds to do that in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The rules say it's either viva voce or it's 92 bis, ter, quater. There's not both. You can't do both. In some other trials, because the counsel are quite incapable of doing their job, they have allowed that and now you're going to follow suit here. Now, you can do what you like, but that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. We need to deliberate to decide whether an accused who is representing himself and who submits a document that is not available in one of the languages of the Tribunal may read out the document or have the witness read out that document and then ask questions to the witness about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. After considering the matter, the Trial Chamber believes that the accused may not -- believes by majority, because I don't share that view, and I'll explain why later. The Trial Chamber believes by majority that the accused may not use a statement taken by the accused in uncertain circumstances that are not similar to that that pertain to a 92 bis statement or by an investigation conducted by an authority, and because this statement lacks a number of items allowing the Chamber to conclude that it's a probative document, this statement may not be read out or used. That's the decision of the Chamber by the majority. I do not share that view for the following reason: I believe that if you have a document drafted by someone who certifies that what he's saying is the truth, if that document has been registered by an authority that is able to certify the authenticity of the signature - I'm not talking about the substance, of course - but under those circumstances I believe that this document, if relevant, may have certain probative value. All the more so since it happens here in this Tribunal that Trial Chambers admit documents without a signature, without an identified author, just because these documents are relevant to the indictment and because these documents have other indicia of reliability. This is, therefore, a decision by the Chamber, by a majority, according to which the accused is not allowed to use that type of document. Secondly, and here I agree with my fellow Judges, when such documents may cast doubt about the witness, the statements should not be read out by the witness himself. Under those circumstances the accused should read out the document and not ask the witness to read out the document. And this is a unanimous decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to correct the transcript. The Presiding Judge said what he wanted to say, but it was not translated properly. He did not talk only about probative value but also of reliability. Let me add that I do not believe in prima facie reliability. I believe that reliability is the proper translation for "fiabilite" in French. The matter of probative value is something different. Here we are more talking about prima facie, reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time has come to have a 20-minute break. I believe that Mr. Seselj has used 1 hour and 40 minutes. He'll have 20 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. You have 20 minutes left, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue with my cross-examination, I have to raise a brief objection, Judges. Previously you objected that I did not mention the sources of my information when I put questions in the course of cross-examination. That was the case with previous witnesses. Now that I've started to show you the sources of my information, you stopped me. But I hope that in future you will not tell me in my cross-examination that I'm failing to report the sources of my information, that you will simply assume that I'm basing my questions on statements made by certain people, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kulic, when you were on trial in Bjelovar in 1995 there were five accused. And your name, what number was it in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Your Honours. I think I was the second or the third indicted, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when you gave a statement before the court and in our courts, both in Serbia and in Croatia, it's always been like this, when there's more than one accused they appear in the courtroom one by one and make statements, and the first one who makes a statement sits down, then another one goes in and makes a statements, and so on and so forth, and then the third one comes in and sits down. So the fifth one did not hear what the four before him said, but the first one in heard what the other four said. So, Mr. Kulic, when you made your statement, why did you ask that the accused who have made statements before you leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember that. I don't remember this fact. It may have happened but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Slobodan Bosanac remembers. He was convicted first to 12 years and then another number of years, 20 years, but I'm not allowed to use the statement. However, I will collect these statements and publish them in my books, and I will give you a gift of a set of books at the end so that you can have a memento of what you prevented from being said in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're saying that Slobodan Bosanac made a statement. Without using that statement, without having it read out, you can say, I have information according to which, and so on and so forth, and then you put a question to the witness. Then later on, as my fellow Judges told you, you can calling Slobodan Bosanac as your witness and he will be able to confirm all of this. Today you can tell the witness that you have information allowing you to state that when he testified he asked for four witnesses to leave the courtroom, and then after that you ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has just said he doesn't remember so why should I put further questions, Your Honours, about this. He doesn't remember, he doesn't remember. Slobodan Bosanac does remember; you're not interested in that, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you were a member of a delegation, you called it a delegation, which signed the Daruvar Agreement in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the signatories of the Daruvar Agreement in 1993, Your Honours. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who authorised you to sign the Daruvar Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time as a civilian I was representing Serbs from the municipality of Podravska Slatina. I was a representative of the Serbs in the municipality of Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does it mean, you were representatives of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a member of parliament. I was a deputy. I was elected by those who lived there, Your Honours, on the territory of Western Slavonia, and that is how I had contacts with the international community. And when there was a proposal that the Daruvar Agreement should be signed, that's the role I played.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, does every member of parliament have the right to enter into these behind-the-scenes activities and say that he is representing the people, that he's a representative, and that he has a right to make such agreements?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no of course not. But it was not the kind of activity Dr. Seselj is alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of activity was it, then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international community was there through UNPROFOR and its organs and in cooperation with a group of us who were then the beginnings of the civilian government that was being established, a proposal emerged that we should move in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did you not inform anyone from the Republic of Serbian Krajina that you were going to those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Daruvar Agreement, at the Assembly of the SAO Western Slavonia was adopted as a document and there were no secrets. That same document was sent to the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. A government session, a cabinet session was held, and although opinions were divided, the cabinet did not support the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, I'm asking you what happened before that. How come you crossed over onto Croatian territory illegally, participated in negotiations with representatives of the Croatian authorities, and the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had no knowledge of it and yet you were a member of parliament of all of Serbian Krajina? So how is this possible?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my working team there were two members of the cabinet and I'm convinced that in the cabinet - I'm still convinced from some information I have, and it's been confirmed to me by some other members of the cabinet - but two members of the government were with me and they signed that agreement together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What two members of the government?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then Deputy Prime Minister, engineer, Zeljko Dzakula and the Minister of Information, Dusan Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were arrested for that reason, all of you together?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was arrested on the 21st of September, 1993, and the agreement was signed I think sometime in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were arrested because of several criminal offences under the Criminal Code of the SFRY, Article 116, paragraph 1, imperilling territorial integrity; Article 118, preventing the struggle against the enemy; and Article 121, paragraph 1, espionage. Was that in your indictment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was no indictment in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what was there, then, in your case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my case there was just an investigation - that's what they said - and the investigating judge who was in charge, he was the only one I knew of and he's still living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were released at the intervention of the occupiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not think, and I still do not think, that the international community is an occupier because it was accepted by the legal organs of Yugoslavia that it should be there. And this way of communicating that Mr. Seselj is using is something I fail to understand and that I don't accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's not up to you to reject or accept anything. You're duty-bound to answer my questions. Did it say in the indictment that you had committed those crimes or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the suspicions about the circumstances Mr. Seselj is putting forward are what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kulic. And this was linked to Article 139, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which says that for these crimes, in a state of war, a death sentence may be handed down. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the law, Your Honours, so I can neither confirm nor deny this. I suppose that's correct. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when in 1995 you were arrested and tried in Bjelovar, you lied and said that the UN had provided you with defence counsel. It was the American embassy in Zagreb that provided you with defence counsel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the UN office in Vienna got me my defence lawyer, Dr. Mihajlo Placar. He arrived in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the accused is addressing a topic that had not escaped my attention. In your written statement of the 11th of May, 2002, you state that you were detained from the 4th to the 8th of May, 1995, and in the second half of the month of May you were assigned counsel and you say that with the assistance -- that it was with the assistance of Mr. Hamilton from the American embassy. Reading this I wondered what the American embassy had to do with your detention. Why did you state that? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try to clarify. When I was arrested in 1995, on the 4th of May in Pakrac, there was a danger. A group of us Serbs there felt that our lives might be under threat. Mr. Peter Galbraith paid special attention to this because he had received some information from the UN about this, and I assume because that's what the representative of the American embassy said - I think his name was Hamilton but I'm no longer sure - he wanted to know how we were being treated and what our accommodation was like, because I had been in a camp for three days and on the fourth day was transferred to the prison. So the only thing this was about was that my friends who were in Pakrac at the time, Mr. Dzakula specifically, insisted with the American embassy that they should check what my situation was, whether I was still alive and what conditions I was in. That was the only reason for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why the American embassy? Why not the embassy of Italy, Zimbabwe, Pakistan? Why the American embassy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on I heard this from some friends of mine, the American embassy had a special attitude towards the Serbian community from before. It contacted mainly through certain individuals. I'm referring primarily to my friend Dzakula, but they had no special interest except to come and check, at Mr. Dzakula's request, to come and see what was happening to me. That's the explanation I got. I had never seen those people before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Dzakula took care of everything, then. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, what role did Hamilton play in the American embassy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours. I think he was a secretary or something like that. He was an employee in the American embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For intelligence, right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. He didn't say that. He didn't introduce himself to me, nor did I ask him about that. I don't think I was of any interest to such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, why did you deny my statement that it was the American embassy that intervened for you and got you your defence counsel when I put that question to you before the Presiding Judge let you see your statement from 2002, which I didn't have time to do?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never received any assistance from the American embassy except for this personal visit when they wanted to find out how I was and convey a message from my friends, and that's all. No more, no less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why didn't you in that statement of 2002 say that it was the United Nations that provided you with defence counsel? Why did you say that only in 2007?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I did say it then. Maybe it's not in the statement. Maybe nobody asked me about it. But there was no reason either then or now for me to keep this secret. I paid partially for my defence. A part was paid by the United Nations, but one part was paid by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were employed, you had a good income, and you were able to pay, right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I have already explained. I worked mostly on humanitarian law with humanitarian organisations, NGOs. But then when I was arrested and later on in Pakrac I was working for the UN office from Vienna regarding the repair of damaged houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After signing the Daruvar Agreement you travelled to Zagreb secretly; is that right? After the signing.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know when I was in Zagreb, whether it was afterwards. It's possible I was there afterwards, but I was in Zagreb. I have no reason to hide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You met with Slavko Degoricija there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met with a group of negotiators, Your Honours, in Zagreb. I think that this group was led by a man called Slavko Degoricija. I don't know him so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he was a high-ranking official in the Croatian government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the Ministry of the Interior. Was he the minister's deputy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he had to do with the interior, Your Honours. There was somebody else there who turned up when the agreement was being signed, a deputy minister. I think his name was Moric or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that was the assistant minister, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe, but Slavko Degoricija was a politician, not a policeman. He didn't have anything to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the services you rendered, the American intelligence service and the Croatian authorities made it possible for you to go unpunished through the Bjelovar trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, and I would like to say again that there are documents, there are records of the trial and the proceedings, and this kind of speculation by Mr. Seselj is completely unnecessary. There's no need to even take it into consideration before this Tribunal because there are official documents which I referred to. I didn't sit there for seven months for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you committed terrible crimes. That's why you sat there. But because of the services you rendered you were released from prison and you were not convicted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the accused and others did things in the Republic of Serbian Krajina which are causing my people to suffer still today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I see you think a lot. Mr. Kulic, in paragraph 51 you said that as of the 1st of June, 1991, up to the 30th of April 1993 you were the deputy president of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Western Slavonia. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 1st of June, 1992, Your Honours, that's correct, until the 30th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 51 it says from the 1st of June, 1991 to the 30th of April, 1993. You signed every page of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I signed it, but I'm telling you the correct dates and this is incorrect, at least that's not correct, what was quoted by Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you misrepresented yourself here saying that you were the deputy president of the Serbian Autonomous District and that that post never existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned paragraph 51 and you give a date. In paragraph 51 we have no date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a date in the second half of that paragraph. It says: "Since between the 1st of June, 1991 to the 30th of April, 1993 I was the vice-premier or vice-president of the SAO," paragraph 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you talking about the statement of the 14th of November 2007?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement from 202 has no paragraphs, it's just a text from start to finish; whereas, in the 207 statement it's been divided into paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to 2002 or 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2007, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version in 2007, in paragraph 51, we have no date, and in addition it is said that he was not deputy president or vice-president but vice-minister, vice-prime minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you look at the Serbian version of paragraph 51. It is 06147723. May we have that version put on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put both versions, B/C/S and English, so that we can see it properly. No, it's not possible? On the ELMO, please, paragraph 51. The registrar does not have the statement. As Mr. Seselj does understand English to some extent, he can see that the month of June is not mentioned in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know English at all, Mr. President. I have the version in Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said you had some understanding. I didn't say that you were fully conversant. I said that you had some understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you show that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever the case may be, the witness does have some understanding of English, and he can see that in the English version the month of June is not mentioned. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't been shown that yet. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed because this is not of any vital importance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is of fundamental importance, as far as I'm concerned. If there's that much difference between the English and Serbian versions, then this has incapacitated my defence. All I'm getting is the Serbian version and the difference here is so great that it really is of vital importance. Now the interpreters can translate that for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. True to fact we can see that in the B/C/S version there is a date, whereas in the English version no mention is made of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, did you sign this statement of yours in Serbian or in English?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that I signed in both languages but I'm not quite sure. But I can understand English sufficiently to see that in many details it does not correspond to the Serbian version, neither does it correspond to the actual state of affairs as they stood.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't see how you think that I can continue my cross-examination like this. Perhaps you think I can, but then explain to me how I'm to go about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that this is important to you. I haven't understood in what way the months of June would be important, so put the question to him and then we will all know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already asked the question: Why did Mr. Kulic falsely represent himself as being the president of the Serbian Autonomous Region when that post did exist.
